a_revoir.message: Stephanie Michele new to the area. Yard was a horror of dead trees and plants. My goal is to provide a restorative environment for the original creatures that dwell here. Believe me, I google all the time, make lists and files on my phone and on paper. I study my yard at all different times of the day to see where the sun shines and for what length of time and what native plants do best. Research how to enrich the soil without using toxic chemicals. I’ve been dreaming of this my entire life. I’m not lazy but to  ask local, experienced gardeners for advice seems the best and most practical way to achieve my goal. But thank you for your suggestion.

a_revoir.message:
Elleira Drassel What “value judgement”?

Again. I urge you to learn something about milkweed and about the collection of the fluff and seeds.

Milkweed is an annual not a perennial. The plant dies at the end of the season. The wind distributes the fluff which have the seed attached. They can drift miles.

By the time the milkweed fluff is harvested, the plant is dead. It is of no value to anyone.

The seeds are knocked off the fluff and distributed in the fields the plants came from to ensure another crop the next year.

The harvesting the seeds ensures that they can be distributed not just from the field they cane from but to home gardens, butterfly gardens…

This is already in practice and has been for years.

What is more dangerous to butterflies is NOT distributing the seeds. And USING the fluff ensures that there are MORE plants to attract Monarchs, not less.

If the demand for the use of the fluff increases it means that MORE fields will be needed and that means that there are more habitats for butterflies.

As for your nonsense about “unscrupulous suppliers preventing plants from reseeding” they don’t need the seeds, they aren’t going out to fields to “harvest” them. It’s time-consuming and there is no “monetization” possible. There’s no “Big Fluff” conspiracy.

Your arguments just not based on facts.
